Nathan Hale was an American patriot and spy for the Continental Army during the Revolutionary War. Executed by the British in seventeen seventy-six, he became a martyr to the cause of independence and an icon of patriotic sacrifice, famous for his purported last words: I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country.

Born in Connecticut, Hale was a Yale-educated schoolteacher who volunteered as a spy for General George Washington after the Battle of Long Island in August seventeen seventy-six. He operated behind British lines in New York, gathering intelligence about British troop strengths, supplies, and positions to assist the American cause.

The British captured him, possibly betrayed by a Loyalist cousin or caught with incriminating papers. He was court-martialed and hanged as a spy at dawn on September twenty-second, seventeen seventy-six. His final words, reportedly I only regret that I have but one life to lose for my country, became a rallying cry for American independence, though the exact wording was recorded by witnesses after his death.

Hale became the first American intelligence casualty and a symbol of patriotic duty, inspiring spy recruitment and sacrifice narratives throughout American history. He never married or had children. His brief life and noble death were overshadowed by the Revolution itself, leaving him a legend rather than a well-documented historical figure.
